attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: Faithful wording, and the borrowing-pledge basis is kept. 'Near-impossible' is firm, high-confidence language that the outcome won't happen, not a medium or low hedge. Labelling the modality 'unlikely' understates it. The 'may not be enough' clause is hedged and is rightly not scored.

contract.note: Counting only SoftBank's own funding and requiring recurring years plus an identified financing constraint is a fair, ordinary reading. No deadline was given, so the horizon is open.

evidence.note: April 2025 SoftBank disclosure. It defines the LTV policy and shows SoftBank's expected effective share was up to $30B. This sets the condition; it is not evidence of the outcome.
Feb 2026 agreement for a further $30B, with the LTV policy unchanged. It is a commitment, not proof of capacity or of inability.
The $30B 2026 follow-on was completed in Oct 2026. That is below $40B but is one year, and it shows no binding constraint. Under the contract it settles neither way.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm forecast with no deadline. SoftBank's own funding was about $30B in each of 2025 and 2026, under $40B, with the LTV policy retained. Nothing shows a financing constraint forced the smaller amount. Nothing shows sustained ~$40B annual funding either. Neither contract condition is met, so the claim is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'likely' and the 'at that rate' assumption. The burn figure is derived from the hedged cost estimate, so it inherits the hedge. Under policy this is probabilistic language and is not scored.

contract.note: The contract applies a plain reading and scoring criteria to hedged language ('it's likely'). Policy does not allow that. It also has to choose between cost, loss and cash-burn readings the speaker blurred.

evidence.note: Secondary report that 2025 revenue was about $13B, which meets the revenue condition. It says nothing about the spending-ratio condition.
CNBC, citing anonymous sources, reports 2025 cash burn of $8B, below $14B. That would weigh against an unhedged burn forecast, but this claim is not scored.
Reports $34B of 2025 spending, above $28B. That is a different measure from cash burn and is context only.

reviews.rationale: Zitron said 'it's likely' that costs are at least $28B, and the $14B burn figure follows from that same hedged estimate. Probabilistic language is not scored. For context only: reported 2025 costs (~$34B) exceed $28B, while reported cash burn (~$8B) is under $14B. The ratio condition is also unestablished.

attribution.note: His own words, made in his own article while discussing his earlier piece on CoreWeave.

semantics.note: 'It is impossible' is firm language. 'This project' refers to CoreWeave's ~1.3GW of contracted capacity. The horizon is end of 2025 and also 2026.

contract.note: Reading 'any of this project is done' as 'no part of it comes online' is the ordinary reading. The 'whole project finished' alternative is flagged but less natural. Excluding the ~360MW already active at end-2024 is fair to the speaker.

evidence.note: Baseline from the S-1 via Bisnow: 360MW active and ~1.3GW contracted at the start of 2025.
Core Scientific had ~500MW contracted to CoreWeave by Oct 2024, delivering in stages through H2 2026.

About 350MW was energized under the CoreWeave contract by Mar 2026. The derived 260MW minimum ignores whatever was already energized at end-2024. Even so, staged delivery makes it likely that some pre-2025 contracted capacity came online.
CoreWeave's active power rose from ~360MW to more than 850MW during 2025. This is a company disclosure and does not break out capacity by contract date.

reviews.rationale: The forecast said no part of the contracted buildout would be done by end-2025 or in 2026. CoreWeave's active power more than doubled during 2025. Core Scientific reports ~350MW energized under a contract that was mostly in place by Oct 2024. Together these meet the contract's early-resolution rule, though attribution to specific contracts is approximate.

attribution.note: The sentence is Zitron's own. The WSJ/S&P quotes that follow are his supporting citations, not the claim.

semantics.note: A present-tense causal claim that OpenAI exposure is materially harming SoftBank. It is faithful.

contract.note: In this ratings and financing context, reading harm as a weakened credit profile, shown by a formal adverse outlook action, is ordinary and fair. Other readings, such as realized losses, could give a different result.

evidence.note: On 2025-04-01, JCR moved SoftBank Group's outlook from Stable to Negative. It cited the $30B OpenAI commitment, Stargate and the rising weight of unlisted AI assets. The rating itself was affirmed, and OpenAI's share of the cause is not separately quantified.

reviews.rationale: Within the April 1-14, 2025 window, an independent agency took a formal adverse credit action, cutting the outlook to Negative. Its rationale centres on the large OpenAI investment and AI-asset concentration. That meets the contract's support condition. Limits: the rating was affirmed, and other AI deals also contributed.
